stories.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
stories.summary: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities By James Landale Reporting from Zaporizhzhia oblast Published 15 September 2026 Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way. His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb. But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta. And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present. "If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can." Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. stories.title: Gaza's bicycle couriers refuse to stop despite danger and pittance pay
stories.summary: Between 40 and 50 workers have died in the Israel-Hamas war at one delivery company alone, yet hundreds remain on the roads, covering routes by bicycle after fuel shortages and the destruction of 74% of Gaza's road network made motorised delivery impossible.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Gaza delivery workers pedalling through rubble on bicycles can spend 40 of their 50-shekel (€12) daily earnings fixing a single puncture.Fuel shortages, transport disruption and the destruction of Gaza's road network have made bicycles — known colloquially as "baskleet" — the primary means of delivery across the Strip.Workers who spoke to Euronews described a job that keeps them under relentless pressure: the physical strain of cycling through rubble, the cost of constant repairs, and the danger of passing daily through areas still under bombardment.In the Maghazi area in central Gaza, Mohammed Abu Amra works for the delivery company Barq.Trips he used to complete by motorbike in under 10 minutes now take him 30 or more by bicycle, with heat, rain, road conditions, and the distances involved making it much more challenging.Tareq Abu Zekri launched Barq during the second ceasefire in January 2025, then expanded by hiring workers who used their own bicycles.When he advertised for riders, 109 applications arrived within a day and a half, among them university graduates with few other options in what remains of the Strip's labour market.The company now has more than 50 employees operat

stories.article_text_excerpt: Russia's largest medical universities are struggling to fill hundreds of postgraduate residency places despite record applications, as new rules requiring graduates to sign advance employment contracts with regional hospitals are deterring candidates.Around 1,500 residency places remain unfilled at major medical universities, according to Russian educational outlet Mel.Moscow's Pirogov University could not fill 289 places, while Sechenov University was short by 211. stories.title: Russia used Claude AI for espionage, disinformation and drone swarms
stories.summary: Anthropic's latest report on the abuse of its AI model found that a Russian-linked hacking group used Claude to automate attacks on more than 20 organisations, including Ukrainian defence ministries and drone suppliers, while separate operators ran pro-Kremlin disinformation in Africa and Moldova.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Russia used Anthropic's Claude AI model to accelerate cyber-espionage operations against Ukrainian and European government targets, run disinformation campaigns in Africa and Moldova, and develop targeting software for autonomous kamikaze drone swarms, the US company said in a report published this month.Anthropic said it had blocked all malicious activity identified in the report, used the findings to strengthen its security systems, and shared the information with government bodies and industry partners.In one major case, a hacking group designated GTG-20006 used Claude to automate operations against more than 20 organisations, including government ministries, defence and intelligence agencies, embassies, think tanks and defence-industrial companies, Anthropic said.Ukraine was the primary target, with suppliers of military drone technology and their supply chains also among those attacked. stories.title: Euronews Debates: unlocking Kazakhstan’s potential as a regional trade hub
stories.summary: At the Astana Finance Days 2026, speakers discussed how Kazakhstan can move beyond its traditional role as a transit country and become a regional hub for production, trade and investment.
stories.article_text_excerpt: At one of the biggest financial forums in Central Asia, Euronews moderated a panel focusing on Kazakhstan drive to turn its position at the heart of Eurasia into more than a transit advantage, by developing logistics, manufacturing and investment.Infrastructure investor Nurzhan Marabayev said efficient, transparent and competitive logistics could unlock new projects across Central Asia. Kazakhstan has relatively low labour, resource and construction costs, he noted, but expensive logistics remain a challenge for the landlocked country.Airport director Meruyert Zholdybayeva highlighted the potential of multimodal transport, citing a China-Europe route that moves goods from Shenzhen to Europe in seven days. She said Aktau could eventually become a major hub combining rail, sea and air links.Manufacturing is also expanding. Alima Issembayeva said production rose from 2.3 trillion tenge in 2021 to almost 4 trillion in 2025, while exports more than doubled between 2021 and 2024.Trade expert Ilya Urazakov cited Kazakhstan’s FDI record and natural resources as key advantages, while Professor Tom Vinaimont stressed the need for currency hedging and predictable financing.
